title: The verb
description: Follow the English verb from its six inflectional forms through auxiliaries, tense, aspect, modality, and the many ways English expresses future time.
example: She may have been reading the report when the call came.

intro: Read *She may have been reading the report when the call came* and count what the clause does at once. It presents the reading as possible rather than actual, places it before the moment of judgement, keeps it in progress, and anchors it against a past interruption. All of that comes from the verb and the small words clustered around it. The verb is the clause’s engine, and a description of English syntax keeps returning to it even when the topic is the noun phrase or the clause.

Two tracks run through the chapter. One follows form: the six inflectional shapes of a lexical verb, the special paradigms of auxiliaries, and the difference between a verb form and the construction it builds. The other follows meaning: tense and time, perfect and progressive, mood and modality, and the several expressions that place a situation in future time.

The tracks meet in the auxiliary chain. Modal, perfect, progressive and passive can stack in a fixed order, each one selecting the shape of the next verb. See that order clearly and the individual meanings stop looking like a list of labels; they become positions in a system a speaker can combine.

blocks.text: *She is writing a novel* and *She began writing a novel* run the same words past the same point, yet the grammar divides them differently. In the first, *is* heads the finite clause and *writing a novel* is its non-finite complement. In the second, *began* heads the finite clause and *writing a novel* is a catenative complement. The predicate of each clause is a verb phrase, its head a verb, and that head decides which other elements are required, permitted or excluded.

So *is writing* is not a constituent. The auxiliary heads one clause; the lexical verb heads a subordinate clause embedded inside it. Longer chains repeat the pattern: *She may have been reading* stacks a modal, a perfect auxiliary, a progressive auxiliary and a lexical verb, each adding a layer rather than a word to a flat string.

*Having finished the report, she left* opens with a participial clause; *to finish the report* is an infinitival one. Both are verb phrases with a verb at the head, and neither carries primary tense on its own. The rest of the chapter separates the forms verbs take from the constructions those forms build.

items.note: Is heads the clause; writing heads the non-finite complement.
Began heads the clause; writing is a catenative complement.
Modal may, perfect have, progressive be, lexical read: four layers.

check.prompt: In She is writing a novel, which word is the head of the finite clause?

options.feedback: Is is the finite auxiliary heading the clause; writing heads its complement.

blocks.text: Line up *take, took, takes, take, taking, taken* and the paradigm looks untidy: six forms, five shapes, and *take* doing duty twice. *Want* and *hit* are untidier still, with syncretism collapsing several forms onto one pronunciation. The grammar nevertheless recognises six positions, because the preterite and the past participle behave differently even when they sound identical.

Primary and secondary forms do different work. A past participle follows perfect *have* and passive *be*; a gerund-participle follows progressive *be* and heads a range of non-finite clauses; the plain form turns up in imperatives, subjunctives, *to*-infinitivals and bare infinitivals. Those are constructions, not further inflectional forms. Calling imperative and subjunctive separate paradigms would mistake a clause type for a shape of the verb.

*He left* is finite; *to leave*, *having left* and *left behind* are not. Finiteness is a property of clauses and VPs, not of verb forms in the abstract. A finite clause is headed by a primary form, or by a plain form in an imperative or subjunctive; a non-finite clause is headed by a gerund-participle, a past participle, or a plain form in an infinitival. Auxiliaries add negative forms such as *isn’t* and *couldn’t*. Modals lack the secondary forms altogether, and *must* has no preterite.

blocks.title: Why participle and adjective are distinct
blocks.text: A word like broken can be a verb form or an adjective. In *It was broken deliberately* it denotes an event and is a passive verb. In *It didn’t look broken* it denotes a state and is an adjective. Tests with objects, seem and degree modifiers help separate the two without relying on the spelling.

check.prompt: Why is the imperative not a separate inflectional form of the verb?

options.text: It uses the plain form, which also appears in other constructions.
options.feedback: Imperative is a clause construction, not a distinct verb paradigm.
Imperatives usually have an understood subject, but that is not the reason.
Imperatives can be negated, with do-support: Don’t be late.

blocks.text: *He has seen it* gives four tests in one clause. Negate it and *not* follows *has* directly; invert it and *has* moves in front of the subject; continue with *and I have too*; stress it and the polarity becomes emphatic. A lexical verb manages none of these without help: *He did not see it*, *Did he see it?*, *He saw it and I did too*, *He DID see it*. Negation, inversion, code and emphasis give the NICE constructions their name, and they identify auxiliaries by syntax rather than meaning.

Dummy *do* is semantically empty. It exists to supply the auxiliary position that those four constructions demand. Because the test is syntactic, *be* counts as an auxiliary even when it merely links subject and complement: *They are cheap* yields *They are not cheap* and *Are they cheap?* Auxiliary *have* behaves the same way, while lexical *have* takes *do*: *They had a fight* gives *They didn’t have a fight*.

*She is writing a novel* does not split into a subject plus a flat *is writing* predicate: *is* heads the clause and *writing a novel* is its complement. Auxiliaries are heads, not dependents. The same analysis explains the shape of questions: *Has she been writing?* moves one auxiliary into the prenucleus and leaves the rest of the clause as the nucleus. Subject-auxiliary inversion is not subject postposing, where a lexical verb precedes its subject, as in *In the corner stood a small table*.

Several kinds of fronted element trigger inversion. Closed interrogatives invert obligatorily; open interrogatives invert when a non-subject wh-phrase is fronted; exclamatives invert optionally. Initial negatives, *only* with clause scope, and *so/such* belong to the same family, and conditional inversion in *Had he seen it, he would have reported it* completes the set.

blocks.title: Test for an auxiliary
steps: Put not immediately after the verb and see whether the result is grammatical.
Form a closed interrogative and see whether the verb can precede the subject.
Add a tag or a code continuation and see whether the verb can stand alone.
Stress the verb and see whether it can carry emphatic polarity.
blocks.conclusion: If the verb passes the NICE tests, it is an auxiliary. If it needs do, it is lexical.

check.prompt: Why is be an auxiliary in They are cheap?

options.text: It takes not and inverts with the subject.
options.feedback: They are not cheap; Are they cheap? The definition is syntactic.
Meaning does not decide the auxiliary class.

blocks.text: Stack the auxiliaries and an order emerges: modal, perfect *have*, progressive *be*, passive *be*, lexical verb. Each one selects the form of what follows. A modal takes a plain form, perfect *have* a past participle, progressive *be* a gerund-participle, passive *be* a past participle. *She may have been reading* therefore reads as modal, perfect, progressive, lexical, with each verb shaping the next.

*She may can swim* fails. Core modals are mutually exclusive in Standard English. The same defectiveness keeps them out of infinitival and perfect positions: *to can swim*, *having could swim* and *has must swim* are all excluded. *Be*, *have* and *do* are not defective in that way, while *need*, *dare*, *have*, *do* and *use* split their time between auxiliary and lexical behaviour.

*She has probably been working* puts *probably* between the perfect auxiliary and its progressive complement; *They may well have been waiting* keeps *may* as head while *well* colours the modal judgement. Adverbs can sit inside the chain without breaking its dependencies.

blocks.text: English marks two primary tenses by inflection, present and preterite, and neither stays inside its obvious time zone. The present can report a timeless truth, a habit, a historic narrative, a scheduled future event, or a future situation in a subordinate clause. The preterite can soften a request, backshift a report, or mark a hypothesis as remote. Form and time are correlated, but the correlation is loose enough to be interesting.

*If I lived there tomorrow* does not put the living in the past; it presents a future possibility as remote. Tense is grammatical; time is semantic. The present typically locates a situation as simultaneous with the time of orientation, the preterite typically as anterior, and context supplies the rest. *I wondered whether you could help* uses the preterite to make the request less direct.

Take *She said she was tired*: *was* is interpreted relative to the past reporting verb, not to the moment of speaking. *He believes she is ill* shifts the reference to his belief rather than the speaker’s present. A single timeline running from the speaker’s now cannot capture those shifts.

blocks.title: Why there is no future tense
blocks.text: Will and shall behave like modal auxiliaries, not like a third tense inflection. They share the syntax and meaning range of can, may and must, and they combine with past and present forms rather than replacing the primary tense system. English expresses future time in many ways, but it does not mark it with a dedicated tense.

check.prompt: What does the preterite signal in If I lived there tomorrow?

options.feedback: The situation is future and hypothetical; the preterite marks its remoteness.
The adjunct tomorrow makes a past-time reading impossible.
The form is not perfective in that sense.

blocks.text: *She has finished* and *She had finished before I arrived* both place a situation before a reference point; the difference is where that point sits. The perfect is the secondary past tense, built from *have* plus a past participle. Its reference point is often the moment of speaking, but it can be a past moment, as in the second example, or a future one, as in *She will have finished by Friday*.

*She has lived in Berlin ever since she married* forces the continuative reading: the living runs from the past up to the reference point. Remove the duration phrase and *She has lived in Berlin* defaults to non-continuative, with the living located at some indefinite time within the relevant span. A duration expression such as *ever since* or *for* usually forces the continuative reading, which is also restricted to atelic situations.

The present perfect differs from the simple preterite by keeping a past situation tied to the present. The tie can be experiential (*I have seen that film*), resultative (*She has written the report*, so the report now exists), or recent (*He has just left*). Past-time adjuncts such as *yesterday* or *two minutes ago* normally exclude the present perfect because they place the situation wholly in the past.

*She may have left* puts the leaving before the modal judgement. *She must have been working* stacks perfect and progressive to present a past ongoing situation inferred from evidence. The order of the auxiliaries keeps those meanings apart: modal first, perfect second, progressive third.

blocks.text: *The flag is red* holds steady; *She walked in the park* goes on without a natural endpoint; *She reached the summit* is over in an instant. Aspect describes that internal temporal shape, and the shape depends on the kind of situation. States are static, like *She knows the answer*. Occurrences are dynamic, dividing into activities, accomplishments and achievements: activities are durative and atelic, accomplishments durative and telic (*She wrote a novel*), achievements punctual.

Multiplicity adds another layer. *She knocked once* is singulary; *She knocked repeatedly* is iterative; *She usually walks to work* is a serial state built from repeated subsituations. A whole can have a different aspectual character from its parts, so a habitual sentence may behave like a state even though every instance is an activity.

Perfective and imperfective aspectuality divide the viewpoint. Perfective presents a situation as a complete whole, seen from outside; imperfective presents it from within, focusing on an internal phase or interval. English marks neither with a dedicated inflection. Simple present and preterite can receive either interpretation, while the progressive is a special imperfective construction.

blocks.text: *She was reading the letter when the phone rang* puts the reading around the moment of the call. *Be* plus a gerund-participle presents the situation as in progress at the relevant time, viewed from within, durative and dynamic. The progressive does more than add duration; it changes the viewpoint, and the change has consequences for what the clause entails.

Entailment and implicature pull in different directions. *I was working* entails *I worked*: an activity in progress has really happened. *She was writing a novel* does not entail that she finished it, though it usually implicates as much. *The train was arriving* stretches a punctual achievement into an approach. Context can cancel the implicatures, but it cannot cancel the entailment.

States generally resist the progressive, which is why *The flag is being red* sounds wrong. The restriction is not absolute, since context can present a state as temporary or dynamic. Nor is the progressive always aspectual. It can supply narrative background, make an interpretation explicit (*I was referring to you*), or present a future arrangement (*We’re meeting tomorrow*).

items.note: Accomplishment in progress: completion is not entailed.
Activity in progress: the activity did take place.
An achievement presented as an approach.
Interpretive use: the progressive clarifies what the earlier words meant.

blocks.conclusion: The progressive is not a general marker of ongoing time. Its meaning depends on the situation and on the surrounding discourse.

blocks.text: *I wish she were here* preserves a fossil: *were* is a residual irrealis form, almost the last inflectional mood English has. The main system is analytic, carried by modals such as *can*, *may*, *must*, *will* and *shall*. Modality itself is broader than those auxiliaries, reaching into adjectives, adverbs, verbs, nouns, clause type and past tense.

Three dimensions organise modal meaning. Strength sets necessity against possibility. Kind separates deontic modality (obligation, permission, prohibition), epistemic modality (commitment to truth) and dynamic modality (ability, disposition and other participant properties). Degree measures how strong the judgement is, and modals can reinforce or clash with one another in modal harmony.

Negation shows how much scope matters. *You mustn’t eat it all* puts the negation inside the modal: it is necessary that you not eat it. *You needn’t eat it all* puts it outside: it is not necessary that you eat it. *May not* and *can’t* repeat the contrast, and the perfect raises the same question in *may have left*.

blocks.text: *She may can swim* fails, and the failure reveals a small, tightly behaved class. The core modals are *can*, *may*, *must*, *will* and *shall*, with *ought*, *need* and *dare* at the edges. They lack secondary forms, *must* lacks a preterite, they take a plain-form complement, and they cannot combine with one another in a single Standard English chain. Their meanings overlap, so one form can carry different kinds of modality in different contexts.

*Must* carries strong necessity, deontic or epistemic. *May* handles possibility and permission; *can* handles ability, possibility and permission with a strong dynamic bent. *Will* stretches from epistemic prediction through dynamic volition to deontic insistence. *Shall* is mainly deontic and formal, at home in first-person offers and suggestions, while *should* and *ought* sit at medium strength, expressing necessity or expectation.

The preterite forms *could*, *might*, *would* and *should* are not simply past tenses. They can mark past time, backshift in reported speech, or modal remoteness. *Could* is the past of *can* in ability contexts, but in *Could you help?* it signals politeness. *Would* can mark habitual past behaviour, a future-in-the-past, or a remote conditional. *Should* has developed idiomatic deontic and evaluative uses that do not reduce to past tense.

blocks.text: Scope decides what a negative or a perfect applies to. *She may not have read it* can mean that it is possible she did not read it, with the negation inside the scope of *may*. *She can’t have read it* normally means that it is not possible that she read it, with the negative outside the modal. The words’ tense has not changed; the structure of the judgement has.

*She may have left* puts the perfect inside the modal’s scope, so the possibility concerns a past leaving. *She must have been working* makes the judgement about a past progressive situation. Reversing the order is not a stylistic preference; it changes which proposition is modalised.

Modal meaning also lives outside the auxiliaries. *Have to*, *have got to*, *be able to*, *be allowed to*, *be likely to* and *be going to* are fixed expressions with modal or future meaning. Lexical verbs such as *permit*, *require* and *insist*, adjectives such as *possible* and *necessary*, adverbs such as *perhaps*, and nouns such as *permission* and *obligation* all belong to the wider modal domain. They differ in register, inflection and syntax even where their meanings overlap with a core modal.

sections.title: Future time without a future tense

blocks.text: English has no future tense, only a repertoire for talking about future time. Modal *will* and *shall*, *be going to*, the present futurate, the progressive futurate, imperatives, mandative clauses and non-finite complements all do the job. *The match starts tomorrow*, *We’re meeting at six*, *She is going to resign* and *I will call you* place a situation in the future by different means.

*Will* is a modal auxiliary, not a tense marker. It expresses epistemic prediction, dynamic volition or deontic insistence, and *would* carries past, backshifted and remote uses. *Be going to* has a stronger present focus: intention, arrangement or imminent development. In the preterite, *was going to* commonly implicates that the intended situation did not happen.

The present futurate handles schedules and planned events: *The train leaves at six*. The progressive futurate presents an arrangement as already under way: *We’re flying to Rome tomorrow*. In subordinate clauses the present often carries future meaning: *If she arrives early, we’ll start*. None of these needs a future inflection, because future time is a semantic relation, not a grammatical category in English.

blocks.text: Tense and aspect do more in a text than locate events. Narrative uses the preterite to carry the main sequence forward and the progressive to supply background: *She was working in the garden when the police arrived*. The perfect ties a past event to a later reference point and often explains a present state: *The road is closed because a tree has fallen*.

The historic present shifts a narrative into the present for immediacy. Backshift anchors a subordinate clause to the reporting time rather than the speaker’s now. Free indirect style moves between these viewpoints without quotation marks. None of these effects needs a new tense form; they arise from tense, aspect and context interacting.

Take *Having finished the report, she left*: the perfect participle places the finishing before the leaving. *With the windows open, the room stayed cool* is a verbless clause describing a circumstance. Non-finite and verbless clauses often have no primary tense at all; the matrix clause, the aspect of the non-finite form and the wider discourse supply the temporal interpretation.

blocks.text: Four systems organise the English verb. Primary tense contrasts present and preterite; secondary tense contrasts perfect and non-perfect; aspect contrasts progressive and non-progressive; mood contrasts modal and non-modal. Each has its own forms and its own characteristic meaning, and all four meet in the auxiliary chain.

That chain runs modal, perfect, progressive, passive, lexical verb. Each auxiliary selects the form of its complement and adds a layer of meaning, while the verb’s subclass decides which complements the clause requires. Tense, aspect and modality are not three names for time; they are separate systems whose interaction produces the temporal and evaluative effects of ordinary prose.

A practical method: find the finite verb, list the auxiliaries in order, then ask what each layer contributes. Is the clause modalised? Is the situation perfect or non-perfect, progressive or non-progressive? Is the verb lexical or auxiliary? Is future time carried by *will*, *be going to*, a present futurate or a subordinate present? Answering those questions turns a long verb chain into a readable structure.

blocks.title: A verb checklist
blocks.text: Find the head of the clause and the auxiliaries that precede it. Check the form selected by each auxiliary. Identify primary tense, then perfect, progressive and mood. Finally, ask what kind of situation the clause describes and how the surrounding discourse anchors it in time.

check.prompt: Which sequence states the auxiliary order correctly?

options.text: Modal, perfect, progressive, passive, lexical verb
options.feedback: May have been being checked follows this order, though such chains are often avoided.

options.text: Perfect, modal, passive, progressive, lexical verb
options.feedback: A modal cannot follow perfect have.

options.text: Progressive, modal, perfect, passive, lexical verb
options.feedback: Core modals precede the other auxiliaries and do not follow be.

worked: Take *She may have been reading the report when the call came*. The finite clause is headed by the modal *may*. Its complement is the perfect clause *have been reading the report when the call came*, whose head is *have*. The perfect takes the progressive clause *be reading the report when the call came* as its complement, and progressive *be* takes the gerund-participle *reading*.

The modal expresses possibility; the perfect locates the reading before the modal judgement; the progressive presents the reading as ongoing at the time of the call. The lexical verb *read* takes the object *the report*, and the adjunct *when the call came* locates the reading in time. Each layer has a distinct job, and the order of the auxiliaries keeps those jobs separate.
application: When you meet a long verb chain, read it from left to right. Identify the first auxiliary, then check the form of the next verb, and continue until the lexical verb. The first auxiliary carries the clause’s primary tense or mood; the later auxiliaries add perfect, progressive or passive meaning.

Next, ask what kind of situation the lexical verb describes. An activity, an accomplishment, an achievement and a state interact differently with the progressive and with duration phrases. The same verb can shift category when its object or complement changes, as in *write a novel* and *write novels*.

Finally, separate form from meaning. A present tense can refer to future time, a preterite can express politeness or remoteness, and a modal can express obligation, inference or ability. The context, the scope of negation and the kind of situation decide which reading is active.
reveal: In *She may have been reading the report when the call came*, *may* is a modal auxiliary expressing epistemic possibility. *Have* marks the perfect, locating the reading before the modal judgement. *Be* marks the progressive, presenting the reading as ongoing at the time of the call. *Reading* is the lexical verb and takes *the report* as its object.
recap: Lexical verbs have six inflectional forms; auxiliaries have special paradigms and special syntax. The NICE constructions identify auxiliaries, and do-support supplies an auxiliary when a lexical verb lacks one. Auxiliaries form a fixed chain: modal, perfect, progressive, passive.

Tense, aspect and mood are separate systems. The perfect is a secondary past tense, the progressive presents an internal view, and modality covers necessity, possibility and related meanings. Future time is expressed by several constructions, not by a dedicated future tense.

self_check.question: Name the six inflectional forms of a lexical verb.
self_check.answer: Preterite, third singular present, plain present, plain form, gerund-participle and past participle.

self_check.question: What are the NICE constructions?
self_check.answer: Negation, inversion, code and emphasis: the four constructions that distinguish auxiliaries from lexical verbs.

self_check.question: What is the difference between the perfect and the progressive?
self_check.answer: The perfect is a secondary past tense locating a situation before a reference point; the progressive is an aspect presenting a situation as in progress and viewed from within.

self_check.question: Why is there no future tense in English?
self_check.answer: Will and shall are modal auxiliaries, and future time is expressed through several constructions rather than a dedicated tense inflection.

self_check.question: What does the preterite often express besides past time?
self_check.answer: Politeness, backshift in reported speech, and modal remoteness in conditionals and wishes.

opening.prompt: Which word is the head of the finite clause in She is writing a novel?

options.feedback: The finite auxiliary heads the clause; writing heads the non-finite complement.
Writing is the lexical verb heading the complement clause.
Novel is the head of the object NP.

opening.prompt: Which property identifies an auxiliary verb?

options.text: It can take not and invert with the subject.
options.feedback: These are the negation and inversion parts of the NICE tests.

options.text: It has a meaning connected with time.
options.feedback: Lexical verbs can also express temporal meaning.

options.text: It always has a past tense form.
options.feedback: Must lacks a preterite, and modals are defective.

opening.prompt: What does the perfect auxiliary have select?

options.feedback: Has written, had gone, may have been seen.
Progressive be selects the gerund-participle.
A modal or supportive do selects the plain form.

opening.prompt: What does the progressive typically present?

options.text: A situation as in progress and viewed from within
options.feedback: Progressive aspectuality is an internal, imperfective view.

options.text: A situation as a completed whole
options.feedback: That is perfective aspectuality, not the progressive.

options.text: A situation located in future time
options.feedback: Future time is a separate interpretation, though the progressive can be used for future arrangements.

opening.prompt: Which statement about future time is correct?

options.text: English expresses future time through several constructions, not a dedicated future tense.
options.feedback: Will, be going to, present futurate and other forms all contribute.

options.text: Will is a future tense inflection.
options.feedback: Will is a modal auxiliary, not an inflection.

options.text: The present tense can never refer to future time.
options.feedback: The present futurate and subordinate clauses routinely do.

closing.prompt: Why can is writing not be analysed as one constituent in She is writing?

options.text: Is heads the finite clause and writing heads a non-finite complement.
options.feedback: Each verb heads its own clause layer.
Writing is a gerund-participle verb heading a complement clause.
Is is an auxiliary.

closing.prompt: What is the difference between mustn’t and needn’t?

options.text: Mustn’t places negation inside the modal; needn’t places it outside.
options.feedback: It is necessary that you not vs it is not necessary that you.
The scope difference changes the obligation.
Both concern present or future necessity.

closing.prompt: Which sentence has a continuative perfect?

options.text: She has lived here for years.
options.feedback: The situation extends from the past up to now.
This is resultative: the report now exists.
This is the perfect of recent past.
The bounded object gives the situation a terminal point.
That is an activity: atelic and unbounded.
That is an achievement: punctual.

closing.prompt: Which construction is a present futurate?

options.feedback: Present tense with future time reference.
Present perfect with present relevance.
Past progressive, not a future arrangement.

predict.prompt: Which word is the head of the finite clause in She has been working?

options.feedback: Has is the finite perfect auxiliary heading the clause.
Been heads the non-finite progressive complement.
Working heads the lexical verb phrase.

guided.prompt: In She may have been reading, what form follows progressive be?

options.feedback: Progressive be selects the -ing form.
The past participle follows perfect have or passive be.
A modal selects the plain form.

transfer.prompt: What does the preterite signal in If I lived there?

options.feedback: The hypothesis is presented as less likely or remote, not as past.
The sentence concerns a present or future hypothesis.
The preterite is not the perfect.

exit.prompt: Which expression is a quasi-modal alternative to must?

options.feedback: Have to expresses necessity but takes do-support and full inflection.
Be going to is primarily a future-time construction.
Be able to corresponds to can, not must.
